summary: Access Software was a Salt Lake City game developer and publisher founded in 1982. Its Commodore-era catalogue included games such as Beach-Head and Raid Over Moscow before the company later became especially associated with the Links golf and Tex Murphy series.
facts: Access Software was founded in Salt Lake City in 1982 by Bruce Carver.
The company was acquired by Microsoft in 1999 and later became known as Indie Built after subsequent ownership changes.
Its early home-computer output included Beach-Head, one of the titles most closely associated with Access during the Commodore 64 era.
note: CCG keeps Access Software's original publisher credit intact even where later budget or regional re-release labels are also recorded.

sources.label: Game Developer — Bruce Carver and Access Software

summary: Accolade was an American game developer and publisher established in 1984. Its home-computer catalogue became particularly well known for sports, driving and action releases, including HardBall! and Test Drive.
facts: Alan Miller co-founded Accolade in 1984 after previously helping to establish Activision.
Accolade operated as a US-based developer and publisher from 1984 until 2000.
Atari acquired the Accolade trademark and a substantial collection of former Accolade game rights in 2023.
note: The archive summary focuses on Accolade's Commodore-era publishing rather than its later console catalogue.

sources.label: Atari — acquisition of Accolade catalogue and trademark

summary: Alligata Software was a Sheffield software house active during the formative years of the British home-computer market. Its releases covered several 8-bit systems, with a substantial presence on the Commodore 64 and BBC Micro.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves a dedicated Alligata Software collection containing home-computer releases from the 1980s.
Its preserved Commodore 64 catalogue includes titles such as Guardian, Who Dares Wins II and Livingstone, I Presume?.
A first-hand account from Dave Palmer places Alligata's beginnings in Sheffield during 1981–82 and identifies Mike Mahony as the person who started the company.
note: The company history combines museum catalogue evidence with a first-hand recollection from an early Alligata participant.

sources.label: Centre for Computing History — Alligata Software collection
The BBC Games Archive — Dave Palmer on Alligata

summary: Alternative Software is a West Yorkshire software publisher whose company record dates from 1986. During the 8-bit era it became strongly associated with inexpensive cassette releases and licensed character games for machines including the Commodore 64.
facts: Alternative Software Limited was incorporated on 4 June 1986.
The company's registered office is in Castleford, West Yorkshire.
Companies House records its business activity as ready-made interactive leisure and entertainment software development.
note: The public facts use the current UK company record; CCG's archive strengths describe the historical games represented on this site.

summary: Ariolasoft was part of Bertelsmann's move into computer software during the 1980s and became an important publisher in the German home-computer market. Its catalogue included numerous imported and licensed titles for systems such as the Commodore 64.
facts: Bertelsmann grouped its computer-software activities into a Digital Information Systems unit during the mid-1980s.
Bertelsmann's corporate history identifies Ariolasoft as the leading publisher in the German home-computer market during this period.
The same expansion coincided with Sonopress beginning duplication of software on floppy disks, datasettes and cartridge media in 1985.
note: Ariolasoft's profile is based on Bertelsmann's own corporate history rather than third-party game databases.

summary: Atarisoft was the Atari publishing label used to bring Atari arcade and console properties to competing home-computer systems during the early 1980s. Commodore 64 releases were sold in the label's distinctive green packaging.
facts: Atarisoft was used by Atari in 1983 and 1984 to publish games for non-Atari home computers and consoles.
Commodore 64 Atarisoft releases used green packaging as part of a platform-specific colour system.
Many Atarisoft conversions were produced by third-party developers while Atari concentrated its internal development on Atari hardware.
note: Atarisoft is kept separate from Atari where the original CCG publisher credit identifies the dedicated label.

summary: Cinemaware was founded by Bob and Phyllis Jacob in the mid-1980s with the aim of combining film and television presentation techniques with computer games. Its visually ambitious releases became particularly associated with the Commodore Amiga.
facts: Bob and Phyllis Jacob founded the company that became Cinemaware in 1985–86.
The business initially used the name Master Designer Software, with Cinemaware becoming the better-known brand and later company name.
Defender of the Crown established the company's cinematic approach on the Amiga and was followed by titles including Rocket Ranger, It Came from the Desert and Wings.
note: The historical description refers to the original Bob and Phyllis Jacob company rather than later businesses that reused the Cinemaware name.

sources.label: Game Developer — Bob Jacob on the Cinemaware era
The Strong Museum — Cinemaware archival collection

summary: Commodore Business Machines grew from Jack Tramiel's typewriter business into one of the defining home-computer companies of the late twentieth century. Its own software publishing accompanied machines including the PET, VIC-20, Commodore 64 and Amiga families.
facts: Jack Tramiel founded the business that became Commodore in 1954 as the Commodore Portable Typewriter Company.
The company was incorporated as Commodore Business Machines in 1955 and later traded as Commodore International.
Commodore launched the Commodore 64 in 1982 and the original company ultimately declared bankruptcy in 1994.
note: This publisher page concerns software carrying a Commodore publisher credit; it is not intended as a complete history of Commodore hardware.

sources.label: Science Museum Group — Commodore Business Machines
